accuracy.evidence: Every probability is computed exactly for X ~ B(30, 0.5) by TAILS.pmf and checked independently in Python with math.comb: P(X ≥ 20) = 0.0494, P(X ≥ 21) = P(X ≤ 9) = 0.0214, P(X ≥ 22) = 0.0081, P(X ≤ 10) = 0.0494, P(X ≥ 20 or X ≤ 10) = 0.0987. So the one-tailed 5% region is X ≥ 20, the two-tailed 5% region X ≤ 9 or X ≥ 21 (actual level 4.28%), two-tailed 10% X ≤ 10 or X ≥ 20, and one-tailed 1% X ≥ 22. The convention of at most α/2 per tail, or equivalently doubling the one-tail p-value, matches the DfE A level content and the Edexcel, OCR and AQA specifications.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the errors examiners' reports repeat for binomial tests: writing a one-sided H₁ for 'biased' (claims scene, prediction 1, challenge 'dir'), comparing a single tail with the whole α in a two-tailed test (split scene feedback 'spends the whole 5% in one tail', 'whole'), judging by how big the count looks ('eye'), choosing the tail after seeing the data (peek simulation, m4, 'peek'), and treating the tail choice as a matter of convenience ('easy').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagtails is about tails: two draggable cut-offs on the B(30, 0.5) bar chart report each tail against α/2 live, the verdict scene shades the one-tailed and two-tailed regions over the same observed X = 20, and a seeded simulation compares a pre-registered tail with a tail chosen after looking. flagsiglev (choosing α, Type I error at a fixed tail) and flagnullh (writing H₀ and H₁) have none of these; the gate measured under 30% source similarity to every lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner finds the region by moving cut-offs until both tail boxes turn green, which shows why X ≥ 20 (4.94%) is too big for a two-tailed tail. Testing 20 heads both ways makes the change of verdict visible before the text explains it. Running rule B shows red false alarms piling up at about twice rule A's rate (8.0% vs 4.0% after 300 runs each, long-run 9.87% vs 4.94%), so the 'decide first' rule is discovered, not just stated.

predictions.evidence: Prediction 1 offers H₁: p > 0.5 for 'the coin is biased', the most common slip. Prediction 2 offers '5% each', which the split scene refuses tail by tail. Prediction 3 offers 'same data, same verdict', disproved by the two shaded regions. Prediction 4 offers '5%, like rule A' for peeking, disproved by the simulation counts.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six why() messages name the slip: one-sided H₁ for an undirected claim (dir), a two-tailed choice for a directed claim (both), comparing with the whole α instead of α/2 (whole), judging by the size of the count (eye), thinking the rule is about easier sums (easy) and thinking the timing does not matter (peek).

readability.evidence: Sentences stay short and every symbol is introduced with words (H₁: p ≠ p₀, 'either way counts'); numbers are given to two decimal places of a percent, the way they appear on calculators. validate_lessons.py readability passed for kid and adult text.

no_filler.evidence: Kid paragraphs: how the claim fixes the tails, how α is split with the actual B(30, 0.5) region, the same data giving two verdicts, and why the choice comes first. Adult paragraphs: specification content, how to read direction words, named mistakes, what the lab does. The content gate found no filler and under 12% overlap with the null-hypothesis and significance-level lessons.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px screenshots in light and dark: the 31-bar chart keeps 0 and 30 axis labels inside the frame, the orange cut-off handles are 24 px circles under the chart, the two tail boxes read 'P(X ≤ 9) = 2.14% ≤ 2.5%' without clipping, the one-tailed and two-tailed tabs sit side by side above the verdict, the two simulation panels each show a 10 by 10 grid with counts and a percentage, and the three tail buttons fit in one row.

accessibility.evidence: Buttons repeat every canvas action: pick a claim then its H₁; lower and upper cut-off minus and plus; one-tailed and two-tailed test; run 100 tests per rule; lower, both or upper tail. Each action writes the full result (probabilities, verdict, counts) to the canvas aria-label and the live region. walk.cjs ran axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) on desktop and iPhone 13 in both themes with no violations.
